claim: Histones are bound to cytosolic lipid droplets (LDs) in Drosophila embryos.
source: We previously discovered histones bound to cytosolic lipid droplets (LDs); here we show that this forms a cellular antibacterial defense system.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by previous work (Cermelli et al., 2006) as cited in the introduction.

claim: In the presence of bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) or lipoteichoic acid (LTA), histones are released from lipid droplets.
source: Sequestered on droplets under normal conditions, in the presence of bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) or lipoteichoic acid (LTA), histones are released from the droplets and kill bacteria efficiently in vitro.
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis showing histone release in response to LPS and LTA treatment (Figure 5A,B).

claim: Droplet-bound histones kill bacteria efficiently in vitro.
source: Sequestered on droplets under normal conditions, in the presence of bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) or lipoteichoic acid (LTA), histones are released from the droplets and kill bacteria efficiently in vitro.
evidence: Supported by colony forming assays and disc diffusion assays showing bacterial killing (Figure 1A-D).

claim: Bacteria grow rapidly when injected into Drosophila embryos lacking droplet-bound histones.
source: Droplet-bound histones also function in vivo: when injected into Drosophila embryos lacking droplet-bound histones, bacteria grow rapidly.
evidence: Demonstrated by GFP-labeled bacteria showing massive bacterial overgrowth in Jabba mutant embryos (Figure 3C).

claim: Bacteria die when injected into embryos with droplet-bound histones.
source: In contrast, bacteria injected into embryos with droplet-bound histones die.
evidence: Shown by decreasing bacterial numbers over time in wild-type embryos (Figure 3C).

claim: Embryos with droplet-bound histones displayed more than a fourfold survival advantage when challenged with four different bacterial species.
source: Embryos with droplet-bound histones displayed more than a fourfold survival advantage when challenged with four different bacterial species.
evidence: Quantified survival data comparing wild-type and Jabba mutant embryos infected with S. epidermidis, E. coli DH5α, L. monocytogenes, and B. subtilis (hlyA) (Figure 3D).

claim: Histones and histone fragments are bactericidal in in vitro assays.
source: While not generally appreciated, histones and histone fragments are surprisingly bactericidal in in vitro assays (Hirsch, 1958).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hirsch, 1958.

claim: In the skin mucosa of catfish, secreted histone H2A contributes critically to the organismal defense against bacteria.
source: For example, in the skin mucosa of catfish, secreted histone H2A contributes critically to the organismal defense against bacteria (Cho et al., 2002), and histones H3 and H4 are prominent antimicrobial agents in sebaceous gland secretions (Lee et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cho et al., 2002.

claim: Histones H3 and H4 are prominent antimicrobial agents in sebaceous gland secretions.
source: For example, in the skin mucosa of catfish, secreted histone H2A contributes critically to the organismal defense against bacteria (Cho et al., 2002), and histones H3 and H4 are prominent antimicrobial agents in sebaceous gland secretions (Lee et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2009.

claim: Excess free histones cause genomic instability, hypersensitivity to DNA-damaging agents, and lethality.
source: In fact, because unconfined histones cause genomic instability, hypersensitivity to DNA-damaging agents, and lethality (Saffarzadeh et al., 2012), cells minimize excess free histones by active mechanisms (Singh et al., 2009a, 2009b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Saffarzadeh et al., 2012.

claim: Cells minimize excess free histones by active mechanisms.
source: In fact, because unconfined histones cause genomic instability, hypersensitivity to DNA-damaging agents, and lethality (Saffarzadeh et al., 2012), cells minimize excess free histones by active mechanisms (Singh et al., 2009a, 2009b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Singh et al., 2009a, 2009b.

claim: Histones have been detected on LDs in C. elegans, fly embryos, moth fat bodies, and mammalian leukocytes, insulin producing β-cells, and muscles.
source: Histones, in particular, have been detected on LDs in a number of animal cells and tissues, including C. elegans, fly embryos, moth fat bodies, and mammalian leukocytes, insulin producing β-cells, and muscles (Cermelli et al., 2006; Wan et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2011; Larsson et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Cermelli et al., 2006; Wan et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2011; Larsson et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2012).

claim: LDs decreased colony forming units (CFU) dramatically for both Gram-negative (Escherichia coli) and Gram-positive (Staphylococcus epidermidis) bacteria.
source: For both Gram-negative (Escherichia coli) and Gram-positive (Staphylococcus epidermidis) bacteria, LDs decreased the CFU dramatically (Figure 1A, compare buffer vs LD), indicating that the droplets have an antimicrobial property.
evidence: Demonstrated by colony forming assays shown in Figure 1A and quantified in Figure 1B.

claim: Alkaline carbonate treatment removes electrostatically bound droplet proteins but not lipids and proteins attached via hydrophobic interactions.
source: This treatment removes electrostatically bound droplet proteins, but not lipids and proteins attached via hydrophobic interactions (Brasaemle et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brasaemle et al., 2004.

claim: Alkaline washes greatly reduced the levels of the electrostatically bound histone H2B, but not of the hydrophobically bound LSD-2.
source: Indeed, as previously reported (Cermelli et al., 2006), these washes greatly reduced the levels of the electrostatically bound histone H2B, but not of the hydrophobically bound LSD-2.
evidence: Supported by citation to Cermelli et al., 2006 and consistent with experimental observations.

claim: Alkaline carbonate-treated droplets no longer had antibacterial activity.
source: These treated droplets no longer had antibacterial activity (Figure 1C, LD-CaCO3), suggesting that the antimicrobial activity requires electrostatically bound proteins.
evidence: Demonstrated by disc diffusion assay shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The antimicrobial activity of LDs requires electrostatically bound proteins.
source: These treated droplets no longer had antibacterial activity (Figure 1C, LD-CaCO3), suggesting that the antimicrobial activity requires electrostatically bound proteins.
evidence: Inferred from the loss of antibacterial activity after alkaline carbonate treatment which removes electrostatically bound proteins.

claim: Mass spectrometry analyses identified histones H2A and H2B as the predominant proteins in the antibacterial region of the gel overlay assay.
source: MS analyses of proteins eluted from this location identified histones H2A and H2B as the predominant proteins present (spectra not shown).
evidence: Stated as a result of mass spectrometry analysis of the gel overlay assay.

claim: The bactericidal activity of LDs is most likely due to histones.
source: Therefore, the bactericidal activity of LDs is most likely due to histones, consistent with their known antimicrobial activities in vitro (Hirsch, 1958).
evidence: Inferred from gel overlay assay results and mass spectrometry identification, supported by citation to Hirsch, 1958.

claim: Pretreatment of purified LDs with anti-histone antibodies abolished or markedly reduced the droplet bactericidal activity.
source: Importantly, pretreatment of purified LDs with anti-histone antibodies abolished or markedly reduced the droplet bactericidal activity (Figure 1A, 1B-LD + Anti-histones).
evidence: Demonstrated by colony forming assays shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: The majority of the in vitro antibacterial activity of LDs from early Drosophila embryos is due to histones.
source: Thus, we conclude that the majority of the in vitro antibacterial activity of LDs from early Drosophila embryos is due to histones.
evidence: Concluded from gel overlay assay, mass spectrometry, and antibody blocking experiments.

claim: Mass spectrometry comparison found no major distinctions in post-translational modifications between droplet-bound and nuclear histones.
source: First, using mass spectrometry, we compared post-translational modifications on droplet-bound and nuclear histones and found no major distinctions, suggesting that unique post translation modifications are not responsible for association of histones to LDs.
evidence: Stated as a result of mass spectrometry analysis comparing droplet-bound and nuclear histones.

claim: Several acetylation sites were identified in histones H2A (serine 1 and lysines 5 and 8) and histone H2B (lysines 7, 11, 14 and 17).
source: We did identify several acetylation sites in histones H2A (serine 1 and lysines 5 and 8) and histone H2B (lysines 7, 11, 14 and 17).
evidence: Stated as a result of mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: Some of the identified acetylation sites were previously found in shrimp histones.
source: Some of these acetylation sites were previously found in shrimp histones (Ouvry-Patat and Schey, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ouvry-Patat and Schey, 2007.

claim: Histones previously examined for antimicrobial activity are reported to be un-acetylated.
source: The histones previously examined for antimicrobial activity are reported to be un-acetylated (Kim et al., 2000), though there was no indication of whether acetylation affected antimicrobial efficacy.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2000.

claim: Droplet-derived histones and commercial pan-histones purified from calf thymus do not differ significantly in antibacterial efficacy.
source: This assay showed that histones are bactericidal and that droplet-derived histones and commercial pan-histones purified from calf thymus do not differ significantly in antibacterial efficacy (Figure 1F).
evidence: Demonstrated by bactericidal activity assays shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Jabba (CG42351) is a novel 42 kDa protein that is a putative histone receptor on droplets.
source: To test the significance of the histones on LDs in vivo, we took advantage of the recent identification of the putative histone receptor on droplets, jabba (CG42351), a novel 42 kDa protein (Li et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2012.

claim: Jabba is present on LDs in wild-type flies and is required for histone localization on droplets.
source: Jabba is present on LDs in wild-type flies and is required for histone localization on droplets; in Jabba mutants LDs are present, but histones are absent from the LDs (Figure 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining and Western blot analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: In Jabba mutants, LDs are present but histones are absent from the LDs.
source: Jabba is present on LDs in wild-type flies and is required for histone localization on droplets; in Jabba mutants LDs are present, but histones are absent from the LDs (Figure 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining and Western blot analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Droplets purified from two different independently isolated Jabba mutant strains displayed essentially no killing activity.
source: Such purified droplets also differed in their antimicrobial activity in vitro: droplets from wild-type embryos resulted in a 10-fold decrease in bacterial growth relative to buffer alone, but droplets from two different independently isolated Jabba mutant strains displayed essentially no killing activity (Figure 2G), as expected if the killing activity of wild-type droplets is indeed due to histones.
evidence: Demonstrated by colony forming assays shown in Figure 2G.

claim: In Jabba mutant embryos, the overall levels of histones are much reduced relative to the wild type.
source: In Jabba mutant embryos, the overall levels of histones are much reduced relative to the wild type (Figure 2F), presumably because the histones not sequestered on the droplets are degraded.
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Histones not sequestered on droplets are presumably degraded in Jabba mutants.
source: In Jabba mutant embryos, the overall levels of histones are much reduced relative to the wild type (Figure 2F), presumably because the histones not sequestered on the droplets are degraded.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of reduced histone levels in Jabba mutants and knowledge that unconfined histones are rapidly eliminated via proteolysis.

claim: Unconfined histones are rapidly eliminated via proteolysis.
source: At least in other systems, unconfined histones are rapidly eliminated via proteolysis (Singh et al., 2009a, 2009b), a protective mechanism against the detrimental effects of free histones.
evidence: Supported by citations to Singh et al., 2009a, 2009b.

claim: Jabba mutants are viable and fertile and develop into apparently healthy adults.
source: Jabba mutants are viable and fertile and develop into apparently healthy adults (though likely with compromised immune systems, see Figure 4).
evidence: Stated as an observation of Jabba mutant phenotype.

claim: Jabba mutant embryos hatch at wild-type rates.
source: In particular, embryos hatch at wild-type rates.
evidence: Stated as an observation of Jabba mutant phenotype.

claim: Buffer-only injection resulted in high and similar hatching success for both wild-type and Jabba mutant embryos.
source: The injection protocol per se does not apparently harm either genotype, since buffer-only injection resulted in high and similar hatching success (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by survival data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Bacterial numbers in wild-type embryos decreased with time after injection.
source: Under the conditions employed, bacterial numbers in wild-type embryos decreased with time (Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by imaging of GFP-labeled bacteria shown in Figure 3C.

claim: 2 hr after injection, approximately 84 bacteria per embryo were present in wild-type embryos.
source: 2 hr after injection, numerous individual bacteria were obvious in the embryos, and we estimate on the order of 84 bacteria per embryo (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: Estimated from imaging data as described in Materials and methods.

claim: By 24 hr after injection, approximately 33 bacteria per embryo were present in wild-type embryos.
source: By 24 hr, the number of visible bacteria had decreased substantially, and we estimate on the order of 33 bacteria per embryo.
evidence: Estimated from imaging data as described in Materials and methods.

claim: By 48 hr after injection, 2-6 bacteria were present in wild-type embryos.
source: By 48 hr, there typically were either no surviving bacteria or only a few detectable bacterial cells, and on average we estimate 2–6 bacteria were present.
evidence: Estimated from imaging data as described in Materials and methods.

claim: Some innate immune mediator(s) limits bacterial cell viability in wild-type embryos.
source: Thus, some innate immune mediator(s) limits bacterial cell viability in wild-type embryos in this experimental system.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that bacterial numbers decrease over time in wild-type embryos.

claim: The limit on bacterial viability was lost in the Jabba embryos.
source: This limit on bacterial viability was lost in the Jabba embryos (Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by imaging showing massive bacterial overgrowth in Jabba mutant embryos (Figure 3C).

claim: 2 hr after injection, approximately 79 bacteria per embryo were present in Jabba mutant embryos.
source: The appearance of multiple individual bacteria 2 hr post-infection was similar to the wild type, and we estimate approximately 79 bacteria per embryo.
evidence: Estimated from imaging data as described in Materials and methods.

claim: By 24 hr after injection, approximately 840 bacteria per embryo were present in Jabba mutant embryos.
source: However, bacterial cell numbers increased dramatically by 24 hr, with 840 bacteria on average.
evidence: Estimated from imaging data as described in Materials and methods.

claim: By 48 hr after injection, thousands of bacteria were present in Jabba mutant embryos.
source: By 48 hr, we estimate that thousands of bacteria were present in the Jabba embryos (Figure 3C, compare WT to Jabbaf07560 at 24 and 48 hr; also see Figure 3—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: Estimated from imaging data shown in Figure 3C and supplementary figures.

claim: Loss of histones on droplets due to the absence of functional Jabba correlates with susceptibility to massive bacterial overgrowth.
source: These results indicate that loss of histones on droplets due to the absence of functional Jabba correlates with susceptibility to massive bacterial overgrowth.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of bacterial overgrowth in Jabba mutant embryos compared to wild-type.

claim: Droplet-associated histones contribute to immunity against introduced bacteria.
source: Because bacterial numbers are controlled, and bacteria are ultimately eliminated in wild-type embryos, it suggests that droplet-associated histones contribute to immunity against the introduced bacteria, consistent with their in vitro bactericidal capability.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of bacterial growth in wild-type versus Jabba mutant embryos.

claim: Injection of bacteria delayed wild-type embryonic development but caused only a minimal increase in lethality.
source: Injection of bacteria delayed wild-type embryonic development, but caused only a minimal increase in lethality, relative to buffer-only injected embryos (normalized survival more than 80%; see Figure 3D, S. epidermidis and E. coli DH5α, orange bars).
evidence: Demonstrated by survival data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: For Jabba mutants, bacterial injection resulted in high lethality with normalized survival of less than 20%.
source: In contrast, for the two independently derived Jabba mutants (both lacking droplet-bound histones; Figure 2D), the same treatment resulted in high lethality, with normalized survival of less than 20% (Figure 3D).
evidence: Demonstrated by survival data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Jabba embryos exhibited at least a fourfold decrease in survival when injected with either E. coli or S. epidermidis.
source: Thus, Jabba embryos exhibited at least a fourfold decrease in survival when injected with either species of bacteria.
evidence: Calculated from survival data comparing wild-type and Jabba mutant embryos (Figure 3D).

claim: At moderate injection dosages of 50-100 bacteria per embryo, there was good survival for wild-type embryos but not for Jabba embryos when infected with B. subtilis or L. monocytogenes.
source: At moderate injection dosages of 50–100 bacteria per embryo, there was again good survival for wild-type embryos, but not for the Jabba embryos (Figure 3D, B. subtilis and L. monocytogenes).
evidence: Demonstrated by survival data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: A marked survival difference between wild-type and Jabba mutant embryos was observed when infected with all bacterial species tested.
source: In conclusion, a marked survival difference between the wild-type (more survival) and Jabba mutant embryos was observed when infected with bacteria, for all of the bacterial species tested.
evidence: Summarized from survival data for all four bacterial species tested (Figure 3D).

claim: Jabba is expressed in a variety of adult tissues and in both sexes, with especially high expression levels in fat body and ovaries.
source: Consistent with a possible role in facilitating stable localization of histones to the cytoplasm, Jabba is expressed in a variety of adult tissues and in both sexes, with especially high expression levels in fat body and ovaries, according to microarray and RNA-seq data available on FlyBase (Chintapalli et al., 2007; McQuilton et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chintapalli et al., 2007 and McQuilton et al., 2012.

claim: Pricking wild-type or Jabba-mutant adults with buffer-dipped needle resulted in low long-term mortality, with roughly 20-30% mortality at 4 days.
source: Pricking either the wild type (black curve, Figure 4A,B) or Jabba-mutant adults (red curves, Figure 4A,B) with the buffer-dipped needle resulted in low long-term mortality, with roughly a 20–30% mortality at 4 days.
evidence: Demonstrated by survival curves shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: At the dose of Listeria used, mortality of pricked wild-type adults was approximately the same as buffer-pricked adults.
source: At the dose of Listeria used, mortality of the pricked wild-type adults was approximately the same as the buffer-pricked adults (the purple mortality curve in Figure 4A is within experimental error of the black curve).
evidence: Demonstrated by survival curves shown in Figure 4A.

claim: For Jabba-mutant adults, pricking with a bacterial-dipped needle was quite lethal, with less than 5% survival at 4 days.
source: However, for the Jabba-mutant adults, pricking with a bacterial-dipped needle was quite lethal (Figure 4A,B, brown curve), with less than 5% survival at 4 days—a 14-fold difference from wild-type survival.
evidence: Demonstrated by survival curves shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: There was a 14-fold difference in survival between wild-type and Jabba-mutant adults when challenged with Listeria.
source: However, for the Jabba-mutant adults, pricking with a bacterial-dipped needle was quite lethal (Figure 4A,B, brown curve), with less than 5% survival at 4 days—a 14-fold difference from wild-type survival.
evidence: Calculated from survival data comparing wild-type and Jabba-mutant adults (Figure 4A,B).

claim: From wild-type or Jabba-mutant adult buffer-pricked cytoplasm, typically less than three bacterial colonies were observed.
source: From wild-type or Jabba-mutant adult buffer-pricked cytoplasm, typically less than three colonies were observed.
evidence: Stated as a result of plate assay using cytoplasmic extract.

claim: For bacterial-pricked adults, initial bacterial counts were typically on the order of 400 CFUs.
source: In contrast, for the bacterial-pricked adults, initial counts were typically on the order of 400 CFUs (Figure 4C), and by day 3 went down significantly for the wild type (50) but less so for the surviving Jabba-mutant flies (320).
evidence: Demonstrated by plate assay shown in Figure 4C.

claim: By day 3, bacterial counts went down to 50 CFUs for wild-type adults but only to 320 CFUs for surviving Jabba-mutant flies.
source: In contrast, for the bacterial-pricked adults, initial counts were typically on the order of 400 CFUs (Figure 4C), and by day 3 went down significantly for the wild type (50) but less so for the surviving Jabba-mutant flies (320).
evidence: Demonstrated by plate assay shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The observed lethality in adult flies correlates with differences in bacterial load.
source: Presumably, the Jabba-mutant flies that died (not assayed) had even higher bacterial counts. While a complete investigation of the kinetics of bacterial load is beyond the scope of this paper, as in the embryos, these results suggest that the observed lethality correlates with differences in bacterial load.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of higher bacterial loads in Jabba-mutant flies compared to wild-type.

claim: The amount of histone H2B detected in cytoplasmic lysates was threefold lower in Jabba-mutant adults compared to wild-type.
source: Compared to the wild-type, the amount of H2B detected was lower in the Jabba-mutant background (threefold), consistent with the embryo data.
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: When purified droplets are incubated in excess buffer, there is no detectable loss of histones from the droplets or appearance of histones in the buffer.
source: Indeed, when purified droplets are incubated in excess buffer, there is no detectable loss of histones from the droplets, or appearance of histones in the buffer (Figure 5A,B, UB control).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Histones are stably bound to LDs.
source: Thus, the histones indeed appear to be stably bound to LDs.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that histones do not dissociate from droplets when incubated in buffer.

claim: The diffusion constant of a 0.5-µm droplet is expected to be much lower than the diffusion constant of a free histone.
source: This might limit their ability to reach the bacteria since the diffusion constant of a 0.5-µm droplet is expected to be much lower than the diffusion constant of a free histone.
evidence: Based on physical principles of diffusion related to particle size.

claim: Bacteria may induce release of histones from droplets.
source: We thus hypothesized that the bacteria may induce release of the histones from the droplets.
evidence: Proposed as a hypothesis to explain how histones can reach bacteria despite being stably bound to droplets.

claim: Organisms often detect bacterial infections due to the presence of LPS or LTA.
source: Indeed, organisms often detect bacterial infections due to the presence of LPS (Heumann and Roger, 2002) or LTA (Wergeland et al., 1989), major pro-inflammatory constituents of Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacterial cell envelopes, respectively.
evidence: Supported by citations to Heumann and Roger, 2002 and Wergeland et al., 1989.

claim: LPS is a major pro-inflammatory constituent of Gram-negative bacterial cell envelopes.
source: Indeed, organisms often detect bacterial infections due to the presence of LPS (Heumann and Roger, 2002) or LTA (Wergeland et al., 1989), major pro-inflammatory constituents of Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacterial cell envelopes, respectively.
evidence: Supported by citation to Heumann and Roger, 2002 and established knowledge.

claim: LTA is a major pro-inflammatory constituent of Gram-positive bacterial cell envelopes.
source: Indeed, organisms often detect bacterial infections due to the presence of LPS (Heumann and Roger, 2002) or LTA (Wergeland et al., 1989), major pro-inflammatory constituents of Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacterial cell envelopes, respectively.
evidence: Supported by citation to Wergeland et al., 1989 and established knowledge.

claim: Histones were detected in the buffer only when LPS or LTA were included.
source: Histones were detected in the buffer (UB, Figure 5A,B) only when LPS or LTA were included, and histone amounts increased with increasing levels of the cell envelope components (Figure 5A,B); concomitantly, histones attached to the LDs decreased (LD, Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Histone amounts in the buffer increased with increasing levels of LPS or LTA.
source: Histones were detected in the buffer (UB, Figure 5A,B) only when LPS or LTA were included, and histone amounts increased with increasing levels of the cell envelope components (Figure 5A,B); concomitantly, histones attached to the LDs decreased (LD, Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Histones attached to LDs decreased when LPS or LTA were added.
source: Histones were detected in the buffer (UB, Figure 5A,B) only when LPS or LTA were included, and histone amounts increased with increasing levels of the cell envelope components (Figure 5A,B); concomitantly, histones attached to the LDs decreased (LD, Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: LPS and LTA induce release of histones from droplets in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Thus, LPS and LTA induce release of histones from the droplets in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: Concluded from Western blot analysis showing dose-dependent histone release (Figure 5A,B).

claim: Histones on LDs are not restricted to Drosophila.
source: Histones on LDs are not restricted to Drosophila.
evidence: Stated as a general observation supported by citations to studies in other organisms.

claim: Specific histones have been identified on LDs purified from a number of mammalian cell lines and tissues.
source: In particular, specific histones have been identified on LDs purified from a number of mammalian cell lines and tissues (Smolenski et al., 2007; Wan et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2011; Larsson et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Smolenski et al., 2007; Wan et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2011; Larsson et al., 2012.

claim: The LD-histone defense system may be widely conserved.
source: Thus, this defense system may be widely conserved.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that histones are found on LDs in multiple species.

claim: The liver removes pathogens and microbial products from the blood and plays a key role in the body's immune response.
source: As a preliminary test, we looked at droplets in the liver, as this organ removes pathogens and microbial products from the blood, and plays a key role in the body's immune response (Mackay, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mackay, 2002 and established knowledge.

claim: The hepatocyte lipid-droplet resident protein ALDI was enriched 103-fold in purified LDs from murine liver.
source: LDs were purified from murine liver using a previously established protocol (Turro et al., 2006); the hepatocyte lipid-droplet resident protein (Turro et al., 2006) ALDI was enriched 103-fold (Figure 6A), confirming the success of the fractionation.
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Histone H1 was detected in the droplet fraction from murine liver using three different specific antibodies.
source: By Western blotting, we detected histone H1 in the droplet fraction, using three different specific antibodies generated in different species (Figure 6B).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The presence of histone H1 on murine liver LDs does not represent contamination with nuclei or chromatin since histones H2A, H2B and H3 were not detectable.
source: This does not represent contamination with nuclei or chromatin since histones H2A, H2B and H3 were not detectable (Figure 6A).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 6A showing absence of other histone types.

claim: Normalized for total protein, the H1 levels on LDs were comparable to the levels of H1 histone in a purified nuclear fraction.
source: Normalized for total protein, the H1 levels on LDs were comparable to the levels of H1 histone in a purified nuclear fraction (Figure 6B—n), and were clearly much higher than in whole-liver homogenates (Figure 6B—h).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: H1 levels on LDs were clearly much higher than in whole-liver homogenates.
source: Normalized for total protein, the H1 levels on LDs were comparable to the levels of H1 histone in a purified nuclear fraction (Figure 6B—n), and were clearly much higher than in whole-liver homogenates (Figure 6B—h).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Histone H1 has antibacterial activity in vitro.
source: Like other histones, histone H1 also has antibacterial activity in vitro (Parseghian and Luhrs, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Parseghian and Luhrs, 2006.

claim: The levels of histone H1 on LDs increased under conditions that mimicked a systemic infection.
source: Intriguingly, the levels of histone H1 on LDs increased under conditions that mimicked a systemic infection.
evidence: Stated as an observation from experiments with LPS-injected mice.

claim: LPS injection resulted in hepatic injury as assessed by increased presence of serum transaminases (AST and ALT) and cytokines (IL-6 and TNFα).
source: LPS injection resulted in the expected hepatic injury (Senga et al., 2008), as assessed by the increased presence of serum transaminases (AST and ALT) and cytokines (IL-6 and TNFα; Figure 6C).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification of serum markers shown in Figure 6C, supported by citation to Senga et al., 2008.

claim: Relative to untreated controls, H1 levels in the lipid-droplet fraction were clearly increased in LPS challenged animals.
source: Relative to untreated controls, H1 levels in the lipid-droplet fraction were clearly increased in the LPS challenged animals (average ratio of H1 in LPS injected to H1 in uninjected was 1.6 ± 0.3 (mean ± SEM), significantly different with a p=0.025 by Student t-test; note that the amount of the lipid droplet marker protein ALDI went down slightly in the LPS-injected samples, and if we use this as a standard, and normalize the detected ratio, it becomes 1.86 instead of 1.6).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis and statistical analysis showing significant increase in H1 levels.

claim: The average ratio of H1 in LPS injected to H1 in uninjected mice was 1.6 ± 0.3 (mean ± SEM), significantly different with p=0.025.
source: Relative to untreated controls, H1 levels in the lipid-droplet fraction were clearly increased in the LPS challenged animals (average ratio of H1 in LPS injected to H1 in uninjected was 1.6 ± 0.3 (mean ± SEM), significantly different with a p=0.025 by Student t-test; note that the amount of the lipid droplet marker protein ALDI went down slightly in the LPS-injected samples, and if we use this as a standard, and normalize the detected ratio, it becomes 1.86 instead of 1.6).
evidence: Stated as a result of statistical analysis of Western blot data.

claim: H1 was efficiently released from murine liver LDs by LPS.
source: Like the Drosophila histones, H1 was efficiently released from the LDs by LPS (Figure 6D), consistent with the hypothesis that the accumulated H1 on the hepatic LDs can be released by the presence of cytosolic bacteria, and thus might contribute to an antibacterial response.
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The accumulated H1 on hepatic LDs can be released by the presence of cytosolic bacteria and might contribute to an antibacterial response.
source: Like the Drosophila histones, H1 was efficiently released from the LDs by LPS (Figure 6D), consistent with the hypothesis that the accumulated H1 on the hepatic LDs can be released by the presence of cytosolic bacteria, and thus might contribute to an antibacterial response.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that LPS releases H1 from droplets, combined with knowledge that LPS is a bacterial component.

claim: Systemic LPS is known to activate numerous defense pathways which could result in increased loading of droplets with histones.
source: In the first case, the systemic LPS is known to activate numerous defense pathways which could then result in increased loading of droplets with histones.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of LPS effects on immune system.

claim: LDs contribute to host defense by sequestration and regulated release of histones.
source: Here, we suggest that LDs contribute to host defense by sequestration and regulated release of histones.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data presented.

claim: Maternal deposition of histone-laden lipid droplets into the embryo may prevent transmission of bacterial infection from mother to egg.
source: Analogous to mammalian mothers depositing antibodies across the placenta into the embryo as it develops, we suspect that maternal deposition of the histone laden lipid droplets into the embryo may prevent transmission of any bacterial infection from mother to egg, and may also protect the embryo from subsequent bacterial infections, resulting, for example, from physical damage to the chorion.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the function of droplet-bound histones in embryos.

claim: Maternal deposition of histone-laden lipid droplets may protect the embryo from subsequent bacterial infections resulting from physical damage to the chorion.
source: Analogous to mammalian mothers depositing antibodies across the placenta into the embryo as it develops, we suspect that maternal deposition of the histone laden lipid droplets into the embryo may prevent transmission of any bacterial infection from mother to egg, and may also protect the embryo from subsequent bacterial infections, resulting, for example, from physical damage to the chorion.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the function of droplet-bound histones in embryos.

claim: The histone-droplet system appears efficient, resulting in a more than fourfold improvement in survival for challenges by multiple types of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, including the known intracellular pathogen Listeria.
source: As tested in the embryos, and in a limited way in adult flies, the system appears efficient, resulting in a more than fourfold improvement in survival for challenges by multiple types of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, including the known intracellular pathogen Listeria.
evidence: Summarized from survival data presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Histones and histone fragments play a role in extracellular antibacterial defense.
source: Histones and histone fragments had previously been reported to play a role in extracellular antibacterial defense (Fernandes et al., 2004; von Kockritz-Blickwede and Nizet, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fernandes et al., 2004 and von Kockritz-Blickwede and Nizet, 2009.

claim: By using histone-droplet sequestration, cells can position histones in the cytosol so they are available to interact with cytosolic bacteria and evade constitutive pathways responsible for degrading free histones.
source: We propose here that by using histone-droplet sequestration, cells can position histones in the cytosol, so that they are both available to interact with cytosolic bacteria, and also can evade constitutive pathways responsible for degrading free histones.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: Any kind of cell has the ability to form LDs.
source: In principle, any kind of cell has the ability to form LDs, and thus employing droplet-bound histones as antibacterial defence might be quite general.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about lipid droplet biology.

claim: Employing droplet-bound histones as antibacterial defense might be quite general.
source: In principle, any kind of cell has the ability to form LDs, and thus employing droplet-bound histones as antibacterial defence might be quite general.
evidence: Inferred from the widespread ability of cells to form LDs and the observation of histones on LDs in multiple species.

claim: Proteomic studies have revealed histones on LDs in tissues from larval and adult insects as well as in a range of mammalian cells.
source: Indeed, proteomic studies have revealed histones on LDs in tissues from larval and adult insects as well as in a range of mammalian cells (Smolenski et al., 2007; Wan et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2011; Larsson et al., 2012), including mouse liver (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations and data from Figure 6.

claim: The role of droplets in the antibacterial response may in part explain why the number and size of LDs increase in disease.
source: Such a role of droplets in the antibacterial response may in part explain why the number and size of LDs increase in disease, from osteoarthritis to liver degeneration and cartilage overproliferation (Tilney and Portnoy, 1989; Bielecki et al., 1990; Lowder et al., 2000; Gunjan and Verreault, 2003; Figueredo et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to studies showing LD increases in disease.

claim: In mammalian leukocytes and macrophages, LDs have been suggested to participate in the regulation of the host response to infection by modulating the production of inflammation mediators like eicosanoids.
source: In mammalian leukocytes and macrophages, LDs have already been suggested to participate in the regulation of the host response to infection, by modulating the production of inflammation mediators like eicosanoids (Bozza and Viola, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bozza and Viola, 2010.

claim: The study discloses an additional role of droplets in innate immunity, a role potentially conserved from flies to mammals.
source: Our result discloses an additional role of droplets in innate immunity, a role potentially conserved from flies to mammals.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings in both Drosophila and mice.

claim: Many medically relevant bacterial pathogens enter the cytosol.
source: Since many medically relevant bacterial pathogens enter the cytosol (e.g. Listeria monocytogenes, Shigella flexneri, Burkholderia pseudomallei, Francisella tularensis and Rickettsia spp; Ray et al., 2009) and histones are also reported to have anti-fungal properties (De Lucca et al., 2011), and many such pathogenic fungi also enter the cytosol (e.g., Cryptococcus neoformans; Bliska and Casadevall, 2009), it may be that the system described here has surprisingly wide utility.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ray et al., 2009 and established knowledge.

claim: Histones are reported to have anti-fungal properties.
source: Since many medically relevant bacterial pathogens enter the cytosol (e.g. Listeria monocytogenes, Shigella flexneri, Burkholderia pseudomallei, Francisella tularensis and Rickettsia spp; Ray et al., 2009) and histones are also reported to have anti-fungal properties (De Lucca et al., 2011), and many such pathogenic fungi also enter the cytosol (e.g., Cryptococcus neoformans; Bliska and Casadevall, 2009), it may be that the system described here has surprisingly wide utility.
evidence: Supported by citation to De Lucca et al., 2011.

claim: Many pathogenic fungi enter the cytosol.
source: Since many medically relevant bacterial pathogens enter the cytosol (e.g. Listeria monocytogenes, Shigella flexneri, Burkholderia pseudomallei, Francisella tularensis and Rickettsia spp; Ray et al., 2009) and histones are also reported to have anti-fungal properties (De Lucca et al., 2011), and many such pathogenic fungi also enter the cytosol (e.g., Cryptococcus neoformans; Bliska and Casadevall, 2009), it may be that the system described here has surprisingly wide utility.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bliska and Casadevall, 2009.

claim: The histone-droplet system may have surprisingly wide utility against both bacterial and fungal pathogens.
source: Since many medically relevant bacterial pathogens enter the cytosol (e.g. Listeria monocytogenes, Shigella flexneri, Burkholderia pseudomallei, Francisella tularensis and Rickettsia spp; Ray et al., 2009) and histones are also reported to have anti-fungal properties (De Lucca et al., 2011), and many such pathogenic fungi also enter the cytosol (e.g., Cryptococcus neoformans; Bliska and Casadevall, 2009), it may be that the system described here has surprisingly wide utility.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the breadth of pathogens that could potentially be targeted.

claim: Histone release from droplets is triggered by bacterial cell envelope components.
source: At least in the case of bacteria, histone release from the droplets is triggered by bacterial cell envelope components.
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments showing LPS and LTA induce histone release (Figure 5).

claim: Histone release allows an appropriate cellular response: freeing enough histones to kill bacteria but minimizing problems of excess free histones interfering with endogenous cellular processes.
source: This release likely allows an appropriate cellular response: freeing enough histones to kill bacteria, but minimizing problems (Gunjan and Verreault, 2003) of excess free histones interfering with endogenous cellular processes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional significance of regulated histone release.

claim: Histone release is achieved via direct binding between LPS and histones.
source: We speculate that this release is achieved via direct binding between LPS and histones, as histones can indeed directly bind LPS (Bolton and Perry, 1997; Augusto et al., 2003) and the presence of LPS did not significantly affect the antibacterial activity of histones in the plate assay.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism supported by citations showing histones can bind LPS.

claim: Histones can directly bind LPS.
source: We speculate that this release is achieved via direct binding between LPS and histones, as histones can indeed directly bind LPS (Bolton and Perry, 1997; Augusto et al., 2003) and the presence of LPS did not significantly affect the antibacterial activity of histones in the plate assay.
evidence: Supported by citations to Bolton and Perry, 1997 and Augusto et al., 2003.

claim: The presence of LPS did not significantly affect the antibacterial activity of histones in the plate assay.
source: We speculate that this release is achieved via direct binding between LPS and histones, as histones can indeed directly bind LPS (Bolton and Perry, 1997; Augusto et al., 2003) and the presence of LPS did not significantly affect the antibacterial activity of histones in the plate assay.
evidence: Stated as an observation from experimental data.

claim: Negatively charged LPS or LTA neutralize the positively charged histones and weaken their electrostatic interactions with Jabba on the LDs.
source: We propose that the negatively charged LPS or LTA neutralize the positively charged histones and therefore weaken their electrostatic interactions with Jabba on the LDs; histone binding to droplets is charge-sensitive, as indicated by the ability of CaCO3 to detach the histones from the droplets.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on charge interactions and experimental observations with CaCO3.

claim: Histone binding to droplets is charge-sensitive, as indicated by the ability of CaCO3 to detach histones from droplets.
source: We propose that the negatively charged LPS or LTA neutralize the positively charged histones and therefore weaken their electrostatic interactions with Jabba on the LDs; histone binding to droplets is charge-sensitive, as indicated by the ability of CaCO3 to detach the histones from the droplets.
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments showing alkaline carbonate treatment removes histones from droplets.

claim: Droplet-bound H1 increases in mouse liver in response to a simulated bacterial infection, suggesting there is a cost to storing histones on droplets.
source: If histones are so effective, why load them not at high levels onto all LDs? The observation that droplet-bound H1 increases in mouse liver in response to a simulated bacterial infection might suggest that there is a cost to storing histones on droplets.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observation that H1 levels increase upon LPS challenge.

claim: Cells likely have to balance immediate histone availability with possible undesirable uncontrolled histone release from droplets due to metabolic consumption of the underlying droplets.
source: Cells likely have to balance immediate histone availability with possible undesirable uncontrolled histone release from droplets due to metabolic consumption of the underlying droplets, or alternatively, potential secondary effects due to the excess histones causing saturation of histone-modifying enzymes (Singh et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the trade-offs in histone storage.

claim: Excess histones may cause saturation of histone-modifying enzymes.
source: Cells likely have to balance immediate histone availability with possible undesirable uncontrolled histone release from droplets due to metabolic consumption of the underlying droplets, or alternatively, potential secondary effects due to the excess histones causing saturation of histone-modifying enzymes (Singh et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Singh et al., 2010.
